source.description: An incident of this source is a Case: same identifier, its alerts the Case's alerts, its evidence the Case's observables.

unknown.name: Informational
unknown.note: the source says nothing; the Case starts at the bottom and triage sets it

resolved.name: Resolved
resolved.note: the source's own closure of its record; the Case is closed by its own verdict, and the two are not the same event

redirected.name: Closed
redirected.note: merged into another incident: the Case closes as a Duplicate of its master

unknown.name: Unknown
unknown.note: the source has not classified the incident, which is how every incident starts and how many are left when they are resolved there

informationalExpectedActivity.name: Benign
informationalExpectedActivity.note: activity that was real and expected: the framework's Benign, authorized activity that legitimately matched the detection

notMalicious.name: Not malicious
notMalicious.note: the one determination a False Positive admits: the activity the detection reported was not there

notEnoughDataToValidate.name: Not enough data to validate
notEnoughDataToValidate.note: Insufficient Data: the checks could not be run or answered, and the record says so rather than claiming a verdict

other.name: Other
other.note: a True Positive or a Benign whose kind none of the words above states

case_map.note: A Case of one incident takes the incident's identifier as its uid. original_event_uid keeps the source's identifier on every Case, a campaign Case among them, whose uid is its own
status_id through vocabularies.status; status_code keeps the source's own word

case_map.ignored: when the source opened its record. The Case's start_time is when the adversary acted, which is the earliest alert activity, and its own lifecycle is in its events

case_map.note: one note for each comment on the thread but this executor's own: a comment it wrote is one of its own Notes written back, which the Case already holds. A writer of Notes to the source also reads the thread so as not to write the same Note twice
the author as the source names them, User- and a person's sign-in name or API-App: and an application's display name: the one name the source gives, and no identity the Case can resolve

priority holds the score as the source writes it, and priority_id is Other (99): the source publishes no thresholds that would place its 0–100 score on OCSF's Low to Critical. A priority set on the Case by other means replaces both, and the score then stays on the source's record

case_map.ignored: who last changed the source's record, as a display name — a person's or an application's. Not an identity the Case can cite, and not a time a poller can resume from

case_map.note: the remark left on the incident when it was resolved in the source. One this executor wrote there is its own closure, which its Note states, and is left out
the tags people put on the incident. The tag this executor puts on the incidents it works is its own mark, and is left out
the source's own tags on the incident

case_map.ignored: the API's own envelope, not the record

case_map.note: In the source's object, an item for each alert that states anything neither OCSF nor the framework carries
In the source's object it names the alert the values beside it belong to

It lands twice. As the severity of the Detection Finding that represents the alert, the event the Alert Observation cites. And as that Observation's confidence (the zerosoc:confidence_id tag: Informational and Low give Low, Medium gives Medium, High and Critical give High) — a workaround, because this source states no confidence of its own for an alert. How bad and how sure are two measures, and the day the source states the second this entry stops borrowing the first.

case_map.ignored: the source's own procedure for the alert, read from its record at triage. It reaches the Case only as the disposition of each recommendation: the Observation a followed one produced, or the Observation that states why it was set aside

case_map.note: first_seen_time only where the alert gives no firstActivityDateTime: the source raised the alert after its activity began, so this is the latest that activity can have started
the workload that raised the alert, by the source's identifier for it. detectionSource, the finer of the two, is the analytic's type

case_map.ignored: the workload's own id for the alert, before Defender gave it one. The Case cites the alert by the id Defender publishes, which is what a reader can open
the alert's back-reference to the incident: the Case is that incident, so the link is the Case's own uid
the tenant, already on the Case once from the incident; an alert of another tenant is not an alert of this Case

case_map.note: A category vocabularies.tactics names is that ATT&CK tactic, on an attack of its own, since the source does not say which of the alert's techniques it goes with. Any other category is kept in the source's object. The framework's alert type is chosen by what the detection fires on and is never read from this

case_map.ignored: the source's per-alert triage state. The Case has one status, and it is the executor's
the source's per-alert verdict. The Case's verdict is the executor's own, and the source's sits on the incident's extension where it is visible without being weighed
as classification: the source's per-alert determination
the source's per-alert assignment. The Case has one assignee, and it is set by the method, not inherited from an alert

case_map.note: the list form of category, read the same way; a word in both is taken once
the source's own tags on the alert, as the values of one tag named systemTags: OCSF gives a tag a key and its values
one note for each comment on the alert's thread but this executor's own, its title naming the alert
as on the incident: the author's display name

case_map.ignored: the state of the source's own automated investigation of the alert. It says whether the product investigated, which bears on who wrote classification and determination; those are recorded and weighed by nobody, and so is this

case_map.note: on a trait of category threat_actor, as the threat's family and name are on one of category malware: an attribution is a lead for the Malicious hypothesis
the policy that generated the alert, a customer's or a built-in one, as an analytic of type Rule (1). detectorId, which every alert carries, is the analytic itself

case_map.ignored: the alert's copy of the incident's link: already on the Case once, from the incident
when the source last changed the alert. A poller resumes from the incident's own time, and the activity times are what the Case's timeline reads
when the alert was resolved on the source. The Case's own closure is the one that counts

case_map.note: a free-form bag the detector may fill, kept whole
what a custom detection reports, as its own key-value pairs, kept whole

case_map.ignored: the entity's kind, as the API types it. It selects which of the fields below are read and becomes the observable's type_id rather than a value of its own
the source's per-entity verdict. Read by the evidence inventory to show what the source thought; it is not an Observation of the Case, which weighs the evidence itself

what the sensor did at the moment of detection: detected, blocked, prevented. It travels with the evidence row the inventory builds, and reaches the Case only inside an Observation that cites it; the state the method reads for §1.5 is remediationStatus
when the source attached this evidence item to the alert — not when the entity acted. The activity times of the alert are what the timeline reads
the part the source gives the entity in the alert. Empty on every item observed; detailedRoles is where the source writes it
the part the source gives the entity in the alert, in its own words. Which entity an Observation is about is decided by the method from the evidence, not taken from a label
the operator's own tags on the entity. Nothing in the framework reads them; a deployment that gives one a meaning records it in the SOC Knowledge Base

the source's identifier for the device, which questions to the source about the device use. The device's observable is its DNS name, and the identifier travels with the evidence row the inventory builds
the device's platform. Asset context the enrichment asks the source for at triage, where it is an Observation with its analytic, rather than an unattributed field on the Case
the device's short name, already in deviceDnsName, which the observable carries
the device's DNS domain, already in deviceDnsName
the device's NT domain. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands

the directory's id for the device. The device is identified by mdeDeviceId and its DNS name. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands
the device's OS build. Asset context: the enrichment asks the source for the device at triage, and what bears on the Case is stated there as an Observation, with its source
the device's OS version. Asset context: the enrichment asks the source for the device at triage, and what bears on the Case is stated there as an Observation, with its source
the sensor's health on the device. Asset context: the enrichment asks the source for the device at triage, and what bears on the Case is stated there as an Observation, with its source
whether the device is onboarded to the sensor. Asset context: the enrichment asks the source for the device at triage, and what bears on the Case is stated there as an Observation, with its source

the state of the anti-malware engine on the device. Asset context: the enrichment asks the source for the device at triage, and what bears on the Case is stated there as an Observation, with its source
the source's own risk level for the device. How much the asset matters comes from the SOC Knowledge Base; the source's score is read at enrichment and stated as an Observation where it bears
the source's device group, by id. An access-control detail of the source, read by nothing
the source's device group, by name. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands
when the sensor first saw the device. Asset context: the enrichment asks the source for the device at triage, and what bears on the Case is stated there as an Observation, with its source

the device's last internal address. Asset context: the enrichment asks the source for the device at triage, and what bears on the Case is stated there as an Observation, with its source; an address an alert cites arrives as evidence of its own
the device's last external address. As lastIpAddress: asset context, and never an observable the Case did not get from an alert
every address of the device's interfaces. As lastIpAddress: asset context, and never an observable the Case did not get from an alert
who was logged on to the device when the alert fired. A lead for the identity pivot of the investigation, asked of the source then and stated as an Observation; not an observable by itself
the name of an account logged on to the device, as loggedOnUsers: a lead for the identity pivot, not an observable
the domain of an account logged on to the device, as loggedOnUsers
the resources the device reached. Empty on every item observed

the cloud virtual machine behind the device, where it is one. Asset context: the enrichment asks the source for the device at triage, and what bears on the Case is stated there as an Observation, with its source
as vmMetadata: the cloud it runs in
as vmMetadata: the cloud's resource path
as vmMetadata: the subscription that holds it
as vmMetadata: the virtual machine's own id
where the source geolocated the address. Geolocation is enrichment and reaches the Case as an Observation with what produced it

where the source places the address. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands; geolocation is enrichment, as countryLetterCode
the network stream the address or the account was seen in. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands

the cloud directory's identifier for the account. The account's observable is its principal name. With userSid and domainName, the identifier tells which directory holds the account, which response needs to know what a connected service can do to it; the framework's Case has no field for that, and an implementation that keeps it does so in its own storage
the account's domain, already in the principal name the observable carries

the account's security identifier. It travels with the evidence row the inventory builds, and reaches the Case only inside an Observation that cites it: it tells a well-known system account from a person's, which the lineage of a process needs

the account's display name. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands; the observable is the principal name
the on-premises directory's id for the account. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands

the account's tenant. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands; the Case carries the tenant once, from the incident
the resources the account reached. Empty on every item observed
where the file was. It travels with the evidence row the inventory builds and with the evidence an Observation rests on; the observable is the hash, which is what a lookup takes
the signature's subject. A check of who signed the file reads it from the evidence row and states it as an Observation, with the check that produced it
the signature's issuer, as signer: read by a check of who signed the file, and not carried unattributed

a second digest of the same file. It travels with the evidence row the inventory builds, and reaches the Case only inside an Observation that cites it, where it helps tell one file from another; the observable is the SHA-256, which every lookup of the method takes
a third digest of the same file, often absent. The observable is the SHA-256
the digest of the file's signature. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier, and listed so that the day the source fills it is a day somebody decides where it lands
the file's size in bytes. Read by nothing
the publisher the source read from the file. As signer: a check of who signed a file states it as an Observation, and it is not carried unattributed
the command line. Evidence an Observation rests on, kept where that Observation cites it, and never an observable: an observable is an entity that can be looked up
the process id, meaningful only with the device and the creation time. The evidence row carries the three together
with processId and the device, the identity of one process instance; on the evidence row, not on the Case as a field
the image's path: with the evidence row, as fileDetails.filePath
as fileDetails.sha1: a second digest of the image, with the evidence row
a third digest of the process image, often absent, as fileDetails.md5. The observable is the SHA-256
the digest of the image's signature, as fileDetails.sha256Ac. Empty on every record observed at this licence tier
the process image's size in bytes, as fileDetails.fileSize. Read by nothing
the publisher the source read from the process image, as fileDetails.filePublisher: stated as an Observation by a check of who signed it, never carried unattributed
the subject of the image's signature, as fileDetails.signer: read from the evidence row by a check of who signed the file
the issuer of the image's signature, as fileDetails.issuer: read with the signer, not carried unattributed
the parent, which the attack graph reads from the evidence rows; on the Case it is an edge, not a field
with parentProcessId, the parent instance; on the evidence row
the parent's image, read with the parent instance on the evidence row
as parentProcessImageFile
as parentProcessImageFile
as parentProcessImageFile: read with the parent instance on the evidence row
as parentProcessImageFile: read with the parent instance on the evidence row
as parentProcessImageFile: read with the parent instance on the evidence row
as parentProcessImageFile: read with the parent instance on the evidence row
as parentProcessImageFile: read with the parent instance on the evidence row
as parentProcessImageFile: read with the parent instance on the evidence row
as parentProcessImageFile: read with the parent instance on the evidence row
as parentProcessImageFile: read with the parent instance on the evidence row

the hive of a registry key or value the alert cites. It travels with the evidence row the inventory builds, and reaches the Case only inside an Observation that cites it: with registryKey it is the identity of one registry entity on one device
the key's path under its hive. With registryHive, the identity of the registry entity on the evidence row
the name of the value under the key. With the key, on the evidence row
the value's data. Evidence an Observation rests on, kept where that Observation cites it, and never an observable
the value's registry type. Read by nothing

extension.description: What this source states about the incident and its alerts that neither OCSF nor the framework carries, kept on the Case under unmapped.microsoft. Anything OCSF or the framework carries is a mapping in the case_map and is never repeated here.

description.description: The source's own narrative of the incident, seeded from the alert that raised it. It says what the incident is about in the source's words, which the per-alert descriptions do not give on their own, so triage reads it as an input the source asserts. It is the source's account and never the Case's: the Case's account is its Notes. A description the executor itself wrote there (its Note and the Case, written back for the analysts who work in the source) is not the source's account and is not read as one (Detection & Analysis §1.1).

summary.description: The source's generated summary of the incident. Like its description, it is the source's account and is read as one.

classification.description: The source's own verdict, recorded and never weighed: the Case's verdict is the executor's.

determination.description: The source's own determination, on the same terms.

assigned_to.description: Who owns the incident in the source; the Case's assignee is the executor's own.

last_update_time.description: When the source last changed the record; a poller resumes from it. OCSF's metadata.modified_time would be the Case's own last change, so it is kept here.

alerts.description: What the source states about an alert and neither OCSF nor the framework carries: one item for each alert that states any of it.

uid.description: The alert, by the uid of its finding_info.

categories.description: The source's categories for the alert that name no ATT&CK tactic, such as SuspiciousActivity or Malware.

custom_details.description: What a custom detection reports, as its own key-value pairs.

additional_data.description: The free-form bag the detector may fill.

asset.cmdb.answers: What is this device: its platform, its risk and exposure, its tags and the value the operator gave it.
limits: a device the endpoint sensor never onboarded is not here

identity.directory.answers: What this source knows about an account: the alerts it appears in and the devices it has used.
limits: this source has no directory record of its own: the account's attributes come from the directory itself, not from here
an account outside the directory — a local account, a guest that never signed in — appears only where an alert named it

malware.repository.answers: What the vendor knows about a file: its own verdict, its signer, and how widely it has been seen.
limits: a hash the vendor has never seen returns no record, which is an answer and not a gap
prevalence is this tenant's and the vendor's, not the world's

reputation.multi_engine.answers: What this source has seen of an address or a domain: the alerts it appears in and its prevalence here.
limits: this is one vendor's sight of the indicator, not a multi-engine consensus: the class is named for what the method wants, and this source answers the narrower question
an address the tenant has never contacted has no statistics, which is not a verdict

cases.store.answers: Has this entity been in an incident before, and how were those incidents determined.
limits: the source's own incident history only, bounded by its retention
an incident's title names the attack, never a device or an account: the entities are in its alerts' evidence, and an incident is matched there

telemetry.endpoint.answers: What ran, what was written, what connected, on a device.
limits: advanced hunting is not available on every licence tier
the hunting tables are retained for 30 days

telemetry.identity.answers: Sign-ins and directory changes for an account.
limits: identity tables are empty where the identity workload is not deployed

process_events.asks: What ran on this device, in this window?
process_events.recipe: DeviceProcessEvents | where DeviceId =~ '{device}' or DeviceName =~ '{device}' | limit {limit}
limits: 30-day retention
advanced hunting is not on every licence tier

file_events.asks: What was written, renamed or deleted on this device?
file_events.recipe: DeviceFileEvents | where DeviceId =~ '{device}' or SHA256 =~ '{hash}' | limit {limit}
limits: 30-day retention

network_events.asks: What did this device connect to?
network_events.recipe: DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemoteIP =~ '{ip}' or LocalIP =~ '{ip}' | limit {limit}
limits: 30-day retention

logon_events.asks: Who logged on to this device, and how?
logon_events.recipe: DeviceLogonEvents | where DeviceId =~ '{device}' or AccountUpn =~ '{user}' | limit {limit}
limits: 30-day retention

registry_events.asks: What was written to the registry on this device?
limits: 30-day retention

sign_ins.asks: Where did this account sign in from?
limits: the table is in preview and absent on lower tiers
sign-in retention is shorter than the endpoint tables on some licences

email_messages.asks: What did this message do, and who else received it?
email_messages.recipe: EmailEvents | where SenderFromAddress =~ '{sender}' or NetworkMessageId =~ '{id}' | limit {limit}
limits: needs the collaboration workload

related_cases.asks: Has this entity been in an incident before?
related_cases.recipe: list_alerts(filter: lastUpdateDateTime ge {since}), each alert's evidence matched on the entity's identifiers (device DNS name or device id; account principal name, security identifier or DOMAIN\name); list_incidents(filter: lastUpdateDateTime ge {since}) for the matching incidents' status and classification
limits: the source's own incidents only
an incident's title names the attack, never an entity: a title match finds nothing
a bare account name is not an identity: the same local account name exists on every machine

directory_changes.asks: What changed on this account or group, and who changed it?
directory_changes.recipe: IdentityDirectoryEvents | where AccountUpn =~ '{user}' or TargetAccountUpn =~ '{user}' | limit {limit}
limits: needs the identity workload deployed against the domain controllers
